spans.content: Image-based Gait Spatiotemporal Parameters Estimation using a Single
Camera and CNN-Transformer Hybrid Network
Ankhzaya Jamsrandorj<sup>1,4</sup>, Quynh Hoang Ngan Nguyen<sup>2,4</sup>, Dawoon Jung<sup>4</sup>, Min Seok Baek<sup>3</sup>, Kyung-Ryoul
Mun<sup>4</sup>, Jinwook Kim<sup>4</sup>
Abstract— Vision-based gait analysis can play an important
role in the remote and continuous monitoring of the elderly’s
health conditions. However, most vision-based approaches com-
pute gait spatiotemporal parameters using human pose in-
formation and provide average parameters. This study aimed
to propose a straightforward method for stride-by-stride gait
spatiotemporal parameters estimation. A total of 160 elderly
individuals participated in this study. Data were gathered with
a GAITRite system and a mobile camera simultaneously. Three
deep learning networks were trained with a few RGB frames
as input and a continuous 1D signal containing both spatial
and temporal gait parameters as output. The trained networks
estimated the stride lengths with correlations of 0.938 and more
and detected gait events with F -scores of 0.914 and more.
Clinical relevance— The proposed method showed excellent
agreements with the GAITRite system in analyzing spatiotem-
poral gait parameters. Our approach can be applied to monitor
the elderly’s health conditions based on their gait parameters
for early diagnosis of diseases, proper treatment, and timely
intervention.
I. INTRODUCTION
Gait can be altered due to injuries, weakness, and aging,
resulting in abnormal walking that can lead to more signifi-
cant health issues such as musculoskeletal, cardiovascular,
and mental health. Accordingly, the gait analysis in the
elderly can be an effective clinical indicator to evaluate
their physical and psychological condition and detect medical
concerns early.
The current specialized systems, including optical motion
capture systems, force plates, and wearable devices, are
expensive, immobile, and inaccessible daily. It may cause
discomfort for the elderly due to the need for high cooper-
ation. Therefore, a vision-based gait analysis system is vital
for evaluating and monitoring the elderly’s gait remotely.
Most vision-based methods focus on the 2D or 3D human
pose estimation with a particular camera system or external
pose machines and then calculate gait parameters based
on skeleton tracking data [1]–[9]. Ismail et al. applied the
DeepPose framework to obtain 2D human joints location
and estimated movements of selected joints with a regression
model for gait analysis [2]. Similarly, Stenum et al. used lat-
eral view videos to measure spatiotemporal gait parameters
by localizing the joints with OpenPose and tracking them [6].
However, the 2D joint locations extracted from the human
pose detector may not be the center of that joints and have
some errors. Besides, 2D pose estimation results are altered
due to view-point, partial occlusion, lighting changes, and
biometric variation. It affects the gait parameters calculation.
Therefore, some research works used 3D joint locations to
avoid these problems and improve reliability for gait analysis.
Azhand et al. proposed a gait analysis system based on
the 3D human poses lifted from the 2D body poses, and
their trackings [7]. Zhu et al. introduced a cascade network
that regressed 3D human joint locations using the infrared
thermal videos and 2D poses extracted from the OpenPose
framework and then calculated gait parameters by tracking
the estimated joints [8]. However, these approaches still
depended on 2D poses and used complicated models to
estimate 3D human joint coordinates. Besides, the methods
were validated on healthy young and older subjects.
In this study, we mainly focus on the elderly, including
healthy controls (HC) and patients with neurodegenerative
diseases, especially Parkinson’s disease (PD), Alzheimer’s
disease (AD), and Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), con-
sidering their high prevalence among the elderly since the
gait can be used to assess neurodegenerative diseases [10]–
[12]. Also, continuous stride-by-stride gait analysis in the
elderly can enable a fundamental clinical assessment of the
risks of injury or fall [9], the effect of rehabilitation after
surgery, and the diagnosis and assess motion disorders.
Hence, this study aimed to propose a vision-based ap-
proach, which does not require human joint locations and
can be easily applied to daily life, for stride-by-stride spa-
tiotemporal gait parameters estimation.
II. MATERIALS AND METHODS
A. Participants
This study is based on work supported by the Institutional
Review Board of the Korea Institute of Science and Tech-
nology.
A total of 160 elderly subjects participated in this exper-
iment. Written informed consent was obtained from all the
participants before the participation. All subjects, including
HC and patients diagnosed with PD, AD, MCI, and other
diseases, could walk without help or aid from devices.

II. MATERIALS AND METHODS
A. Participants
This study is based on work supported by the Institutional
Review Board of the Korea Institute of Science and Tech-
nology.
A total of 160 elderly subjects participated in this exper-
iment. Written informed consent was obtained from all the
participants before the participation. All subjects, including
HC and patients diagnosed with PD, AD, MCI, and other
diseases, could walk without help or aid from devices.

characteristics of each study group.
B. Experimental protocol
The data were simultaneously collected from an indoor
environment with a GAITRite walkway system and a mobile
camera, as shown in Fig.1. The participants were instructed
to walk on the pressure mat at their preferred speed. The
participants were requested to carry out the walking action
ten times. A camera recorded the walking action from a
lateral view with a resolution of HD and a frame rate of
30 Hz. Ground truths of gait spatiotemporal parameters,
including stride length (SL), foot contact (FC), and foot-
off (FO) times, were measured by the GAITRite walkway
system. The videos and data from the GAITRite system were
manually synchronized by an expert using the first FC event,
and another expert then cross-checked the synchronizations.
C. Gait spatiotemporal parameters estimator development
1) Target construction for vision-based gait spatiotempo-
ral parameters estimation: The GAITRite system provides
two groups of spatiotemporal gait parameters: average pa-
rameters in the test field and individual-footfall parameters
in the detailed field. We extracted time information on which

FC and FO events occur and SL from each participant’s
individual-footfall parameters, and every SL parameter was
normalized using the participant’s leg length. As shown in
Fig.2, these spatiotemporal parameters were used to construct
the stride-by-stride 1D signals for vision-based estimation.
The stride length is the distance between consecutive mo-
ments of FC of the same foot. However, we built the
1D signals between FO and FC events of the same foot.
Assuming the participants had consistent velocity during
the walks, the signal was linearly increased to reach the
ground truth of SL extracted from the GAITRite system.
Accordingly, each constructed signal contains both spatial
and temporal gait parameters of each stride.
2) Network architectures: The proposed network, CNN-
Transformer, for vision-based gait spatiotemporal parameters
estimation consisted of a spatial feature extractor, a temporal
feature extractor, and fully connected layers. The ResNet18
pre-trained on ImageNet was adopted as the spatial feature
extractor from the input frames, and the transformer encoder
was used to extract temporal features. As shown in Fig. 3,
the input feature sequences insinuated positional information
and fed it to the transformer encoder, which contained two
encoder layers. Each encoder layer had four multi-head
self-attention sublayers and a feed-forward layer. The final
module has two fully connected layers with a ReLU activa-
tion function and Dropout between them. We conducted the
experiments with two deep learning networks of the Long
Short-term Memory (CNN-LSTM) and the Bidirectional
LSTM (CNN-BiLSTM) as the temporal features extractor
for the performance comparisons. The networks’ input is 27
subsequent video frames, and the output of the networks is
the constructed target values of the stride lengths for both
legs.
D. Implementation details
1) Data processing: The networks’ input was the twenty-
seven subsequent frames with the ground truth human bound-
ing boxes and the constructed stride length values for all
frames. The raw frames were preprocessed by cropping the
person in the frame, then pad left and right to get a square
image and resize it to a 448×448. We divided the dataset into
three parts by subjects. The training set included data from
96 participants, consisting of 20 AD, 17 MCI, 21 PD, 15
HC, and 23 subjects with other diseases. The validation set
contained data from 32 participants, including 7 AD, 5 MCI,
8 PD, 5 HC, and 7 subjects with other conditions. Finally,

3) Training scheme: Pytorch framework was used for all

E. Evaluation metrics
The target for gait spatiotemporal parameters estimation
was designed as simple 1D signals. MAE (cm) and intraclass
correlation coefficient (ICC) were used to evaluate the net-
works’ performance for stride lengths estimation. The peak
values, which define the stride length, were first picked for
each signal, and then the MAE and ICC of type (2,k) were
calculated to assess the agreement between the GAITRite
system and the proposed method. F<sub>1</sub>-score (F1) was used
to evaluate networks’ performance for gait events detection.
We found the frames with peak values to precise the frame
numbers containing FC events. The closest points with a
threshold of 2 (cm) determine frame numbers with FO
events. Then the frame difference between the target and
the prediction frame numbers was calculated. If the frame
difference was less than a threshold of 2 frames, the event
was treated as a true positive. All other gait event predictions
were considered false positives, and all targets that were not
detected were treated as false negatives.
III. RESULTS
The estimation results were illustrated in Fig.4, showing
that all three networks accurately estimated stride lengths
and detected the frames with gait events.
Table II summarized the MAE and ICC of the deep
learning networks for estimating the right and left stride
lengths. The CNN-Transformer network achieved the min-
imum MAEs of 6.909 and 7.420 on the stride lengths esti-
mation. Accordingly, the highest ICCs were 0.962 and 0.957,
acquired by the CNN-Transformer network in estimating the
right and left stride lengths, respectively.
Table III summarized FO and FC events detection results
of the networks on the test set. For all networks, the detection
performance of the FO event was higher than that of the FC
event. The CNN-Transformer network achieved the highest

IV. DISCUSSION
This study introduced a novel vision-based approach for
spatiotemporal gait parameters estimation. We constructed
the simple 1D signals containing both spatial and temporal
gait parameters for continuous stride-by-stride gait analysis.
The deep learning networks trained with a few RGB frames
achieved promising performance in estimating spatiotempo-
ral gait parameters through the constructed signals. It is
worth noting that our approach does not require any special
sensors, markers, or human pose estimators for gait analysis
in the elderly.
The proposed approach showed excellent agreement with
the GAITRite walkway system in analyzing spatiotemporal
gait parameters. The best estimation performance that the
CNN-Transformer network achieved in this study might have
derived from its ability to simultaneously access the long-
range sequential data using the multi-head self-attention
mechanisms. Unlike the CNN-LSTM, the CNN-Transformer
network can consider both future and past information simul-
taneously, which also brings the benefit of CNN-BiLSTM,
with two times less computation cost.
Using the CNN-Transformer network, we analyzed esti-
mation performance on different subject groups, including
AD, MCI, PD, and HC. As shown in Table VI, the CNN
Transformer network estimated the stride lengths with the
ICC of 0.929 and more and detected FO events with the
\mathrm { F } _ { 1 }
-scores of 0.933 and more regardless of subject groups.
However, the FC events for AD and PD patients were
detected inadequately compared to HC and MCI. Based on
the estimation performance, the proposed approach can be
used for the remote monitoring and analysis of not only
normal but also pathological gait.
As mentioned in the introduction, most vision-based meth-
ods use human pose estimation machines to locate human
joints and track them to compute spatiotemporal parameters.
However, some studies used only RGB videos for gait
analysis. Yu and Jeong et al. developed and used the same
deep learning network for analyzing gait. They estimated

estimated the stride-by-stride gait parameters without any
preprepared features, making it more appropriate for con-

to their health conditions, the elderly and the patients may
have distinguishable gait characteristics at different stages of
walking, such as the starting, middle, and ending phases. The
stride-by-stride spatiotemporal gait parameters can enable the
analysis of gait variability at these walking phases.
Several things may be considered limitations in this study.
This study aimed to detect gait events and estimate the stride
length only. The temporal gait parameters can be computed
using the main two gait events. However, more spatial param-
eters, such as step length, width, and foot clearance, will be
considered in future work. Our approach achieved promising
performance for gait spatiotemporal parameters from the
single-view videos. Still, extending the proposed method

IV. DISCUSSION
This study introduced a novel vision-based approach for
spatiotemporal gait parameters estimation. We constructed
the simple 1D signals containing both spatial and temporal
gait parameters for continuous stride-by-stride gait analysis.
The deep learning networks trained with a few RGB frames
achieved promising performance in estimating spatiotempo-
ral gait parameters through the constructed signals. It is
worth noting that our approach does not require any special
sensors, markers, or human pose estimators for gait analysis
in the elderly.
The proposed approach showed excellent agreement with
the GAITRite walkway system in analyzing spatiotemporal
gait parameters. The best estimation performance that the
CNN-Transformer network achieved in this study might have
derived from its ability to simultaneously access the long-
range sequential data using the multi-head self-attention
mechanisms. Unlike the CNN-LSTM, the CNN-Transformer
network can consider both future and past information simul-
taneously, which also brings the benefit of CNN-BiLSTM,
with two times less computation cost.
Using the CNN-Transformer network, we analyzed esti-
mation performance on different subject groups, including
AD, MCI, PD, and HC. As shown in Table VI, the CNN
Transformer network estimated the stride lengths with the
ICC of 0.929 and more and detected FO events with the
\mathrm { F } _ { 1 }
-scores of 0.933 and more regardless of subject groups.
However, the FC events for AD and PD patients were
detected inadequately compared to HC and MCI. Based on
the estimation performance, the proposed approach can be
used for the remote monitoring and analysis of not only
normal but also pathological gait.
As mentioned in the introduction, most vision-based meth-
ods use human pose estimation machines to locate human
joints and track them to compute spatiotemporal parameters.
However, some studies used only RGB videos for gait
analysis. Yu and Jeong et al. developed and used the same
deep learning network for analyzing gait. They estimated
average spatiotemporal parameters using preprepared fea-
tures extracted from RGB video frames with the 3D CNN
network [13], [14]. Compared to these studies, our approach
estimated the stride-by-stride gait parameters without any
preprepared features, making it more appropriate for con-
tinuous and remote gait analysis in daily life. Besides, due
to their health conditions, the elderly and the patients may
have distinguishable gait characteristics at different stages of
walking, such as the starting, middle, and ending phases. The
stride-by-stride spatiotemporal gait parameters can enable the
analysis of gait variability at these walking phases.

Several things may be considered limitations in this study.
This study aimed to detect gait events and estimate the stride
length only. The temporal gait parameters can be computed
using the main two gait events. However, more spatial param-
eters, such as step length, width, and foot clearance, will be
considered in future work. Our approach achieved promising
performance for gait spatiotemporal parameters from the
single-view videos. Still, extending the proposed method
with multi-view videos, enhancing the network architecture
to improve the performance, and examining different shapes
of the target signal are in the future work plan.

V. CONCLUSIONS
This study proposed a vision-based approach for stride-by-
stride gait spatiotemporal parameters estimation. Our results
support the ability of the proposed method to assess various
gait. The deep learning networks trained with a few video
frames and continuous signals as targets showed competitive
performance in detecting gait events and estimating stride
lengths. Our approach can be applied to monitor the elderly’s
health conditions in their homes and contribute to early diag-
nosis of diseases, proper treatment, and timely intervention.
